note: What each driver makes of the codes its robot's maker defines, in four classes — DRY-COVERAGE-PLAN.md 12.C.6, the dry proxy for layer 9. ok: healthy (no flag, a zero fault word, commands taken). degraded: running with something wrong (DEGRADED alone, commands taken). fault: the robot is not doing what it is told (FAULT and DEGRADED, commands refused — DEGRADED because §27's rhal condition reads that bit and not FAULT). estop: the maker's stop chain is open (ESTOP and DEGRADED, commands refused). A vocabulary has a kind: an alarm channel's unlisted code escalates (unmapped) to fault or estop, never to ok or degraded; a warning channel — codes the maker documents as advisory — may stop at degraded. probes are codes chosen outside every table, which tools/fault-vocab/contract.py injects and holds the driver to; no_probes says why a vocabulary has none (a bitset or a total decode has no value outside it). fault_code says how the fault word relates to the code: verbatim (the injected code), derived (the subject says how — node << 16 | code for CANopen, a drive's ring position plus one for EtherCAT), or absent (the vocabulary has no code of its own to carry, only the flags). Every code names the maker's own word for it; source says where the table comes from, what was generated from the maker's own source, what was measured against the maker's software and what was only read. not_covered lists a vocabulary or state the driver reads that this table does not cover, with the reason; pending is a driver that is not bound yet and says why; table_of is a Rust port held to its Python twin's table by a test of its own that reads this file. A driver with no entry at all is a check failure (tools/check-fault-vocab.mjs): silence is not an answer. This table is a statement about translation, not about the robot: it says what a driver does with a code, never that the code means what the maker says it means on the machine in front of you.

safety_status.source: Universal Robots' RTDE guide, `safety_status`, which numbers the safety modes 1 to 9 as below; the driver's own SAFETY_NAMES says the same. The names were checked against the maker's own controller: URControl in universalrobots/ursim_e-series (2026-10-01) carries a SAFETY_MODE_ string for each of the nine, and for fourteen more (AUTOMATIC_MODE_SAFEGUARD_STOP, BRAKE_PIN_FAILURE, IMMI_EMERGENCY_STOP, IMMI_SAFEGUARD_STOP, PROFISAFE_AUTOMATIC_MODE_SAFEGUARD_STOP, PROFISAFE_EMERGENCY_STOP, PROFISAFE_SAFEGUARD_STOP, PROFISAFE_WAITING_FOR_PARAMETERS, SAFETY_API_SAFEGUARD_STOP, SAFETY_PLANES_SAFEGUARD_STOP, SYSTEM_THREE_POSITION_ENABLING_STOP, TP_THREE_POSITION_ENABLING_STOP, UNDEFINED_SAFETY_MODE, VALIDATE_JOINT_ID) that this table does not number. NOT measured: the integers. The binary gives names and no numbers, and URSim cannot be put into any state but NORMAL without its GUI, so the numbering is the guide's, read, and not the controller's, measured.

3.why: the arm is stopped and its program halted until a person unlocks it; a servo target is ignored

4.why: a safety limit was violated; the arm moves only under manual recovery, not under a program

5.why: a safeguarding device stopped the arm; it does not run a program until released

safety_status.unmapped_because: (0 is not probed: a zero fault word is §24's healthy, so a state numbered 0 could not be carried verbatim by any driver.) This is the safety system's own state. A value the driver has never heard of is a safety state it cannot read, and the most restrictive thing it can honestly say about one is that the stop chain is not known to be closed. Reporting it as healthy, or as merely degraded with commands still taken, is the answer a person standing next to the arm cannot afford.

not_covered.why: a mode other than RUNNING already sets DEGRADED with no fault word, and whether each mode (BACKDRIVE, UPDATING_FIRMWARE, POWER_OFF …) is a refusal of commands or not is a statement about the controller this table has not been made to; the fault word carries the safety status only, so a mode would need a second word §24 does not have
it names the same states as text, and `open()` refuses on anything but NORMAL — including REDUCED, which is a working state; that is the conservative direction and is not covered here

error_code.channel: the controller's `error_code`, in the rich report (10 Hz) and the control socket's GET_ERROR
error_code.source: UFACTORY's own `ControllerErrorCodeMap` (xArm-Python-SDK `xarm/core/config/x_code.py` at d911319cebc45142613e18086aabb8067b18ab7f, the pin sim/Dockerfile builds): 41 numeric codes, each with the vendor's title, generated from the SDK and not retyped; the SDK's own `other` entry is the unlisted case. Measured against the maker's firmware: only that an error and a code 41 are reported (F181, UFACTORY's simulator image); the table's classes are read, not measured — the maker's firmware raises these on motion this repository cannot make.
error_code.why: an xArm that holds an error is stopped: the controller enters its STOP state, which the driver reports as ESTOP, with FAULT beside it for the cause and DEGRADED for §27, which reads that bit. Only codes 1 to 3 are the maker's emergency-stop circuit; the rest stop the arm for another reason. They are one class here because the driver reads the stop from the controller's state, and an arm the controller has stopped is a stopped arm to the OS whichever code stopped it. A person cleans the error; the driver never does (bridge.py).

error_code.unmapped_because: the vendor's own table ends in `other`: an error the controller raises that its documentation does not list. It is still an error, and an arm holding one is stopped; reading it as anything milder would be the driver deciding an unknown code is harmless.

warn_code.channel: the controller's `warn_code`, in the rich report (10 Hz)
warn_code.source: UFACTORY's own `ControllerWarnCodeMap`, same file and commit: 5 numeric codes, each with the vendor's title, generated from the SDK; the SDK's own `other` entry is the unlisted case. Read, not measured.
warn_code.why: a warning is advisory: the controller runs on. The driver reports it as DEGRADED and keeps taking commands. The fault word carries the warning code when no error is held, and the flags say which kind it is — DEGRADED alone is a warning, FAULT beside ESTOP is an error — because §24 gives the black box one word.

13.name: User command control code does not exist

14.name: User instructions and parameters have no solution

warn_code.unmapped_because: the vendor's own table ends in `other`. An unlisted warning is not read as healthy, because the driver cannot say what it is a warning about, and is not read as a stop, because the maker documents warnings as advisory.

errors.channel: the 41 `errors` flags of the FCI robot state (a fixed array, one byte each, at offset 1290), one-based in the order below
errors.source: Franka Robotics' own `research_interface::robot::Error` enum and `getErrorName` (libfranka-common `include/research_interface/robot/error.h` at 2e090a65e51c94a98f9fc82b6ec3d1aa54d0f85f): 41 enumerators in wire order, the names the vendor's own function returns, generated from the header and not retyped. A code here is the enumerator's index plus one, which is what the driver's fault word carries (§24: zero is healthy). Read, not measured: the maker's controller raises these on motion this repository cannot make.
errors.why: any set error flag is the controller having aborted the motion and entered its Reflex mode: the arm is not doing what it is told until a person (or `automaticErrorRecovery`) recovers it. The driver never clears one (F26's rule at a second vendor). It is a fault and not a stop: the maker's stop is the separate USER_STOPPED robot mode, below.
errors.unmapped_because: any set flag is a fault, whichever it is, so an index nobody has heard of is read the same way.
errors.no_probes: the wire carries exactly 41 flags in an array whose size is part of the protocol version the driver refuses to mismatch at open, so no value outside the table can arrive; a forty-second would be a new protocol version, and a refusal at open, not a code

robot_mode.channel: the FCI robot state's `robot_mode` (one byte, at offset 1372)
robot_mode.source: Franka Robotics' own `research_interface::robot::RobotMode` (libfranka-common `include/research_interface/robot/rbk_types.h`, same commit): kOther, kIdle, kMove, kGuiding, kReflex, kUserStopped, kAutomaticErrorRecovery, in that order from zero. The class of each is read, not measured.

0.name: kOther
0.why: a mode the maker names only as other: the driver cannot say the arm is doing what it is told

3.name: kGuiding
3.why: the arm is being guided by hand; the FCI does not move it

4.name: kReflex
4.why: the controller aborted a motion; the arm is not doing what it is told until recovered

5.name: kUserStopped
5.why: a person's stop at the Control box: the maker's stop chain is open

6.name: kAutomaticErrorRecovery
6.why: the controller is recovering the arm and takes no motion until it is done

robot_mode.unmapped_because: a mode this driver has not heard of is one it cannot say the arm is doing what it is told in. It is not read as a stop: that is the maker's word for kUserStopped, and nothing says an unknown mode is it.

emcy_error_code.channel: the emergency object a drive sends when something in it changes: COB-ID 0x080 plus the node, the emergency error code in its first two bytes (little-endian)
emcy_error_code.source: CiA 301's emergency error code table, as CANopenNode's `CO_EMC_*` lists it (`301/CO_Emergency.h` at 9b8beed8367241e96ac03f916cd5a500bcb2cf23, Apache-2.0): 35 codes, generated from the header and not retyped, the name each carries being the header's own comment. A table of classes and a few specific codes, not of every code a drive may send: CiA 402's own additions (0x7305, incremental sensor 1 fault, which `slave.py`'s `fault()` sends) and every manufacturer-specific code are not in it, and are the unlisted case. Read, not measured: a drive raises these on events this repository cannot cause.
emcy_error_code.why: an emergency object is an event, not a state: it says something changed in the drive, and the drive may go on running (an over-temperature warning) or may already have faulted (the statusword says which, and is the other vocabulary). Either way the black box wants the code, and the OS wants to know the drive is not well, so a drive with a standing emergency is DEGRADED and the fault word carries the node in its upper half and the code, verbatim, in its lower: `node << 16 | code`. An emergency with the code 0x0000 is CiA 301's error reset, and clears it.

33072.name: 0x8130 Life Guard Error or Heartbeat Error

33296.name: 0x8210 PDO not processed due to length error

33328.name: 0x8230 DAM MPDO not processed destination object not available

emcy_error_code.unmapped_because: an emergency code in no table — CiA 402's, a manufacturer's — is still a drive saying something is wrong. It is not read as healthy, and not as a stop, because the statusword is what says the drive has stopped and the emergency object does not.

statusword_state.channel: the statusword (0x6041) in TPDO2, decoded by CiA 402's own mask-and-value table; the code here is the canonical statusword a drive in that state publishes, with the voltage bit
statusword_state.source: CiA 402's state machine, as `skynet_canopen/cia402.py` decodes it (`state_of`) and `slave.py` publishes it (`statusword_for`); the decode is total, so no statusword is unlisted. Read, not measured.
statusword_state.why: CiA 402 names eight states and this table lists three: the one a drive works in, and the two a person has to clear. The other five (not ready to switch on, switch on disabled, ready to switch on, switched on, quick stop active) are left out on purpose and are listed under not_covered.

15.name: fault reaction active
15.why: the drive is bringing itself to a stop after a fault and applies no command

8.name: fault
8.why: the drive has latched a fault and applies no command until a person resets it; the driver never does (F26)

statusword_state.unmapped_because: unreachable by construction: CiA 402's decode matches every statusword to one of the eight states
statusword_state.no_probes: CiA 402's state decode is total — the last row of its table masks to zero and matches every statusword the rows above it did not — so there is no value outside the table to probe

not_covered.what: the five CiA 402 states a drive is in when it is not enabled and not faulted (not ready, switch on disabled, ready to switch on, switched on, quick stop active)
not_covered.why: the driver brings a drive back to operation enabled itself — `write_command` sends the enable-operation controlword on every cycle, and that is the whole of `release_stop`'s recovery after a stop left every drive in quick stop — so refusing commands on these states would stop the recovery they exist to allow. The state is how the driver gets back to enabled, not a statement that the drive is not doing what it is told; whether a drive that stays in one of them is, is the next question, and it is a measurement of the drive and not of the driver

not_covered.what: object 0x603F, the drive's own error code, and 0x1001, its error register
not_covered.why: they are read by SDO, which is acyclic: a read inside `read_state` would block the cycle on a bus transaction. The emergency object carries the same code unprompted and is covered above

statusword_state.channel: the statusword (0x6041) in the cyclic input image, decoded by CiA 402's own mask-and-value table; the code here is the canonical statusword a drive in that state publishes
statusword_state.source: CiA 402's state machine, as `skynet_canopen/cia402.py` decodes it (`state_of`), which this driver shares with `drivers/canopen`; the decode is total, so no statusword is unlisted. Read, not measured.
statusword_state.why: the same three states `drivers/canopen` lists, for the same reasons. The fault word is the drive's position on the ring plus one, because the cyclic image carries the statusword and not the drive's own error code (0x603F), which is read by CoE and is acyclic — see not_covered.

15.why: the drive is bringing itself to a stop after a fault and applies no command

8.name: fault
8.why: the drive has latched a fault and applies no command until a person resets it; the driver never does (F26)

statusword_state.unmapped_because: unreachable by construction: CiA 402's decode matches every statusword to one of the eight states
statusword_state.no_probes: CiA 402's state decode is total — the last row of its table masks to zero and matches every statusword the rows above it did not — so there is no value outside the table to probe

not_covered.what: the drive's own error code (0x603F) and the CoE emergency message
not_covered.why: both travel by the mailbox, which is acyclic: a read inside `read_state` would block the cycle on a mailbox exchange (and §4's first rule is that it does not block). The simulated slave serves 0x603F, so the code is there for a driver that reads it off the cycle; this one does not, and the fault word says which drive faulted and not why. This is the gap CANopen's emergency object closed for CANopen, and EtherCAT's equivalent needs the mailbox serviced on a thread of its own

not_covered.what: the five CiA 402 states a drive is in when it is not enabled and not faulted
not_covered.why: as `drivers/canopen`: the master brings a drive back to operation enabled itself, so refusing commands on them would stop the recovery they exist to allow

not_covered.what: the application-layer state (INIT, PRE-OP, SAFE-OP, OP) and its AL status code
not_covered.why: a slave that leaves OP stops processing outputs, and the working counter is what the master reads for it (a drive that falls off the ring is `MasterError`, `EIO`); the AL status codes (ETG.1000) are a vocabulary of their own and a separate table

mav_state.channel: HEARTBEAT.system_status (MAV_STATE), read by `read_state` off the latest heartbeat of the one vehicle the driver is bound to
mav_state.source: MAVLink's common dialect, MAV_STATE: nine values. Their names, numbers and the one-line descriptions quoted in `why` are read from pymavlink 2.4.49's generated common dialect (`pymavlink/dialects/v20/common.py`), and `make check-layout` holds the driver's names and numbers to it when it is run, which CI does not do per push. The classes are this table's reading and are not measured: that ArduPilot reports CRITICAL or EMERGENCY while one of its failsafes is flying the vehicle is read, not seen, and no firmware was made to report CRITICAL, EMERGENCY, POWEROFF or FLIGHT_TERMINATION (the SITL suite never provokes them).
mav_state.why: MAV_STATE is the autopilot's own account of what it is doing, and the one thing in a heartbeat that says a failsafe has fired. The first three values are 'not up yet' (degraded: the vehicle itself refuses to arm and says so, and the motions are taken as far as it allows); STANDBY and ACTIVE are the two healthy ones; CRITICAL, EMERGENCY and POWEROFF say the vehicle is flying its own failsafe, is losing the airframe or is shutting down (fault); FLIGHT_TERMINATION is the autopilot ending the flight, which is as final a stop as the maker has (estop).

0.name: MAV_STATE_UNINIT
0.why: the dialect says 'state is unknown': a vehicle that has not said what it is doing is not known to be well, and is not stopped either

1.name: MAV_STATE_BOOT
1.why: the dialect says the system is booting up: not flight-ready, and the vehicle refuses what it cannot do in its own words

2.name: MAV_STATE_CALIBRATING
2.why: the dialect says the system is calibrating and not flight-ready

5.name: MAV_STATE_CRITICAL
5.why: the dialect says a non-normal flight mode in which the system can however still navigate; ArduPilot's failsafes are what put it there, so this reads it as a failsafe the vehicle is flying itself. It is not doing what this driver last asked, and a new motion would fight the failsafe; the way out (`hold`, `rtl`, `land`, `disarm`) stays open

6.name: MAV_STATE_EMERGENCY
6.why: the dialect says a non-normal flight mode in which the system lost control over parts or the whole airframe, in mayday and going down: nothing it is asked to do can be relied on, and `land` and `disarm` are what a person has left

7.name: MAV_STATE_POWEROFF
7.why: the dialect says the power-down sequence has begun and the system will shut down now: there is no better class for a body about to be gone, and a motion it will not hear is not accepted

8.name: MAV_STATE_FLIGHT_TERMINATION
8.why: the dialect says the system is terminating itself: the autopilot ending the flight, motors cut, a parachute or a fall. Read as the maker's stop chain, closed for good, and nothing moves the body

mav_state.unmapped_because: MAV_STATE is one byte and the dialect defines nine of its values: a vehicle that reports another is firmware this table was not written for, and the state of an autopilot nobody has described is not read as healthy
mav_state.keeps_because: a vehicle in a failsafe is moved by what the person asks of it and not by joint commands: `hold` and `rtl` and `land` are how a vehicle is brought down or to rest, and `disarm` (with force=1 in the air, the driver's own rule) is the last thing a person has when the airframe is lost. A driver that refuses them because the heartbeat says CRITICAL has taken the way out away at the moment it matters; a flight termination refuses them with the rest, because there is nothing left for them to move

not_covered.what: SYS_STATUS's sensor-health bitmask and battery level
not_covered.why: a bitmask and a percentage, not a code vocabulary: the driver reads three of the sensor bits and a battery at or below 10 percent as DEGRADED and nothing worse, and the suite holds each by its own check; there is no value outside a table to probe
read only to put the vehicle's own words into a refusal, never as a health state of the body, so the translation this table holds does not touch it

not_covered.what: the autopilot's flight modes (ArduPilot's custom_mode numbers) and the failsafe a vehicle is flying
not_covered.why: a mode number is not a fault: which failsafe is flying is in a mode the vehicle chose (RTL, LAND, BRAKE) and in a STATUSTEXT, and the driver's mode table is held against the firmware by the SITL suite; the one thing a failsafe puts in the heartbeat's state word is the CRITICAL this table covers

system_fault_severity.channel: `SystemFault.severity` of every fault in `system_fault_state.faults` (the faults that are active now; `historical_faults`, which the maker says have cleared, are not read), in `GetRobotState`
system_fault_severity.source: Boston Dynamics' own `robot_state.proto` (boston-dynamics/spot-sdk, master, fetched 2026-10-01, sha256 678766f6928b568c…): the enumeration's names and numbers are generated from `bosdyn-api` 5.2.0's compiled descriptors, which the driver's own client imports, and the one-line descriptions quoted in `why` are the proto's comments. Nothing here was measured against the maker's robot. Boston Dynamics ships no simulator of the gRPC API, and the fake in this tree reports whatever the suite tells it to, so the table's classes are read from the maker's descriptions and never seen on a robot.
system_fault_severity.why: the maker says an active system fault is an indicator of a hardware or software problem that 'may indicate the robot may fail to comply with a user request' — a failure to enable motor power, a loss of perception, a fault recovery behaviour — and gives the severity as the indication of how bad. Read as three classes: INFO is no problem (ok), WARN is a robot that may perform worse (degraded), and CRITICAL, or a severity the maker has not graded, is a robot that cannot be relied on to do what it is told (fault). In `fault` the driver refuses the motions that take the body somewhere new (`power_on`, `stand`, `selfright`) and still answers `stop`, `sit` and `power_off`. When several faults are active the worst class wins and the fault word is that fault's own `code` — Boston Dynamics' number for the variety of fault, 'useful for Boston Dynamics support staff to diagnose' it — so the black box carries what a person can look up.

0.name: SEVERITY_UNKNOWN
0.why: the maker's 'Unknown severity': a fault the robot did not grade is read as one that could be critical, and not as harmless

1.name: SEVERITY_INFO
1.why: the maker's own description is 'No hardware problem': the OS is not told the robot is impaired because it has something to say

2.name: SEVERITY_WARN
2.why: the maker's own description is 'Robot performance may be degraded': running, with something wrong, which is DEGRADED and nothing worse

3.name: SEVERITY_CRITICAL
3.why: the maker's 'Critical fault'; of a battery fault at this severity the maker's field comment says the robot is 'likely' going to shut down immediately

system_fault_severity.unmapped_because: the enumeration is the maker's and a robot newer than bosdyn-api 5.2.0 may grade a fault with a value this table has never seen: a fault the driver cannot grade is read as the worst grade the maker defines, and never as an information message
system_fault_severity.keeps_because: Spot is moved by what a person asks of it and not by joint commands (its joints are read-only, §59.2). With a critical fault `stop` holds the robot where it is, `sit` brings it to the ground and `power_off` cuts the motors: the three things a person has when a fault says the robot may shut down, and a driver that refuses them because the state says critical has taken the way out away at the moment it matters

behavior_fault_cause.source: Boston Dynamics' own `robot_state.proto` (boston-dynamics/spot-sdk, master, fetched 2026-10-01, sha256 678766f6928b568c…): the enumeration's names and numbers are generated from `bosdyn-api` 5.2.0's compiled descriptors, which the driver's own client imports, and the one-line descriptions quoted in `why` are the proto's comments. The refusal is the maker's own statement about the message: behaviour faults 'would block any robot commands from going through', and the command service answers `STATUS_BEHAVIOR_FAULT` ('The robot must not have behavior faults'). Nothing here was measured against the maker's robot. Boston Dynamics ships no simulator of the gRPC API, and the fake in this tree reports whatever the suite tells it to, so the table's classes are read from the maker's descriptions and never seen on a robot.
behavior_fault_cause.why: whatever the cause, the maker says a behaviour fault blocks robot commands until an operator clears it through `ClearBehaviorFault`, which this driver never calls. That is the robot not doing what it is told, so every cause is `fault`; the driver refuses the motions that take the body somewhere new before the robot does, and passes the rest to the robot, which refuses them itself. The fault word is `0x80000000 | cause`: the maker has no code for a behaviour fault (its `behavior_fault_id` is only the handle `ClearBehaviorFault` takes), so the cause is what a person can look up, and the top bit says which message it came from.

1.name: CAUSE_FALL
1.why: the maker's 'Error caused by mobility failure or fall'

2.name: CAUSE_HARDWARE
2.why: the maker's 'Error caused by robot hardware malfunction'

3.name: CAUSE_LEASE_TIMEOUT
3.why: the maker's 'A lease has timed out'

4.name: CAUSE_COMMAND_FAILURE
4.why: the maker's 'A command failed in a way that it cannot autonomously recover from'

behavior_fault_cause.unmapped_because: the enumeration is the maker's and has grown (the fifth value, a command failure, is newer than the others): a cause this table has never seen is still a behaviour fault, which the maker says blocks commands
behavior_fault_cause.keeps_because: the maker says a behaviour fault blocks every robot command, so `stop` and `sit` are refused by the robot itself and no driver can answer them. `power_off` is a call to the power service and not a robot command, and it is what a person has: motors off, the robot safe to approach, and then the fault to be cleared. A driver that refuses it because the state shows a fault has left the robot powered with nothing to do about it

estop_state.channel: `EStopState.state` of every slot in `estop_states`, in `GetRobotState`: the driver's own endpoint and every other the robot lists, a hardware button included
estop_state.source: Boston Dynamics' own `robot_state.proto` (boston-dynamics/spot-sdk, master, fetched 2026-10-01, sha256 678766f6928b568c…): the enumeration's names and numbers are generated from `bosdyn-api` 5.2.0's compiled descriptors, which the driver's own client imports, and the one-line descriptions quoted in `why` are the proto's comments. Nothing here was measured against the maker's robot. Boston Dynamics ships no simulator of the gRPC API, and the fake in this tree reports whatever the suite tells it to, so the table's classes are read from the maker's descriptions and never seen on a robot.
estop_state.why: an estop slot that is not released is the robot's stop chain open: the maker says it cannot power its actuators. The driver reads a slot in any state but the released one as the stop, so a state the maker has not defined cannot read as a stop that is released, and it refuses every motion while it holds. The driver's own CUT (`emergency_stop`) is a separate latch and is not this table.

0.why: the maker says no E-Stop information is present and that this 'only happens in an error case': a robot that cannot say its stop is released is not read as released

1.name: STATE_ESTOPPED
1.why: the maker says the robot cannot power its actuators

2.name: STATE_NOT_ESTOPPED
2.why: the maker says the robot may be able to power its actuators: the stop is released

estop_state.unmapped_because: the maker defines three values and says one of them, unknown, is an error case: a slot that says anything but 'released' is a stop chain that is not known to be closed, and an unknown state of a safety system is read as the most restrictive thing the driver can honestly say

Nothing here was measured against the maker's robot. Boston Dynamics ships no simulator of the gRPC API, and the fake in this tree reports whatever the suite tells it to, so the table's classes are read from the maker's descriptions and never seen on a robot.
motor_power_state.why: the one value that is a fault is the error state, which the maker says must be powered off before the robot is powered again; until then a motion cannot be answered, so it is read as `fault` and the driver refuses the motions that bring the body up. The others are the motors' ordinary states and the two transitions somebody asked for. The fault word is `0x40000000 | state`, the maker's number for it with a marker that says which message it came from.

0.name: MOTOR_POWER_STATE_UNKNOWN
0.why: the maker marks this value 'Unknown motor power state. Do not use this field.': a robot that reports it has not said what its motors are doing

1.name: MOTOR_POWER_STATE_OFF
1.why: the maker says 'Motors are off, the robot is safe to approach'

2.name: MOTOR_POWER_STATE_ON
2.why: the maker says 'The motors are powered'

3.name: MOTOR_POWER_STATE_POWERING_ON
3.why: the maker says the robot has received an ON command and is turning on: a transition this driver or an operator asked for

4.name: MOTOR_POWER_STATE_POWERING_OFF
4.why: the maker says the robot is powering down and is 'not yet safe to approach': a transition somebody asked for, and not a fault

5.name: MOTOR_POWER_STATE_ERROR
5.why: the maker says the robot 'is in an error state and must be powered off before attempting to re-power': motors that will not take a command until they are powered off

motor_power_state.unmapped_because: the enumeration is the maker's and a value this table has never seen is a motor state the driver cannot say is safe to command
motor_power_state.keeps_because: the maker's own way out of the motor error state is to power off before powering on again, so `power_off` is the one motion a person needs; a driver that refuses it has taken the only recovery away

not_covered.what: `PowerState.shore_power_state` and the battery's charge and temperature
not_covered.why: a charger connection and a percentage are not a code vocabulary the driver translates into a class: nothing in `read_state` looks at either, and there is no value outside a table to probe; a battery fault arrives as a system fault with the `battery` attribute and is covered by its severity
free strings: the severity is what grades a fault, and the name and the diagnostic code are for a person reading the maker's documentation, which the fault word's `code` already points them to

not_covered.what: `RobotCommandResponse` and `PowerCommandFeedback` statuses (the robot's answers to a motion)
not_covered.why: answers to a request, not a state the robot is in: the suite holds each by a check of its own (refused as EPERM when the robot says it is faulted or not powered, EIO when the answer is not a success) and there is no state to inject for the contract to read

feetech_status.channel: the Feetech `Status` register (STS3215), read by the bridge's 100 ms health poll through LeRobot's own FeetechMotorsBus; a reading counts when two polls in a row agree (F271)
feetech_status.source: Feetech's own `scservo_sdk` (`protocol_packet_handler.py`: the `ERRBIT_*` constants and `getRxPacketError`'s strings), as installed by `lerobot[feetech]==0.6.1`. Read, not measured: the emulator stages the bits.
feetech_status.why: any error bit is a servo that has shut itself down or is about to: FAULT and DEGRADED, and commands refused until it clears, because a servo in error ignores the goal it is given and answering OK would be success the driver did not have.
feetech_status.unmapped_because: the bridge reports any bit it reads, named or not, and a bit the maker added later is still a servo in trouble; the word carries it verbatim in the low half so the black box keeps what the table could not name. Bit 7 is unstageable on this bus for a separate reason — the maker's own SDK discards any reply whose error byte exceeds 0x7F as a framing error before the bits are read — so the subject reports it not injectable per code rather than staging a packet the library would drop

dynamixel_hw_error.channel: the Dynamixel `Hardware_Error_Status` register (address 70), read by the bridge's 100 ms health poll through LeRobot's own DynamixelMotorsBus; a reading counts when two polls in a row agree (F271)
dynamixel_hw_error.source: ROBOTIS's e-manual, XL430-W250, `Shutdown(63)` — the register `Hardware_Error_Status(70)` defers to for what each bit is — read 2026-10-05. The voltage page says `0x10` where the Shutdown table and its worked example (0x05 is voltage 0x01 and overheat 0x04) say bit 0; the table is the reading used here and the page's figure is a vendor-doc inconsistency, recorded rather than followed. Read, not measured: the emulator stages the bits.
dynamixel_hw_error.why: any error bit is a servo the maker says shuts its torque off: FAULT and DEGRADED, and commands refused until it clears, because a servo whose drive has let go ignores the goal it is given and answering OK would be success the driver did not have.

ros2_base.pending: nothing to cover: ROS 2 defines no fault vocabulary for a mobile base. `nav_msgs/Odometry` carries none; `diagnostic_msgs/DiagnosticStatus` has four levels (OK, WARN, ERROR, STALE) but its names, hardware ids and key-value pairs are each robot's own free text, and not every base publishes `/diagnostics` at all (ros2_control's diff_drive_controller does not). The driver reads none of it and the fault word stays 0; what it does read is what a stop is worth: a base told to stop that the odometry still shows moving `stop_settle_s` later reads FAULT, and odometry that has stopped arriving reads ETIMEDOUT and DEGRADED (held by `drivers/ros2_base/selftest.py`). Revisit with a `/diagnostics` subscription when a base is run that publishes one, so that its levels can be mapped to the four classes

ros_industrial.pending: nothing to cover: ROS-Industrial's simple_message defines no fault vocabulary. RobotStatus carries an `error_code` that is each controller vendor's own number (MotoROS's, abb_driver's and fanuc_driver's are three tables the protocol does not name) beside tri-state flags (drives powered, e-stopped, in error, in motion, motion possible); the driver reads the flags and the code, puts the code in the fault word verbatim and maps no meaning onto it. What the flags do is held by `drivers/ros_industrial/selftest.py` (an e-stop, an error held as a flag or as a code alone, drives off and motion impossible are each refused at open and refuse a command, and an error is FAULT and DEGRADED and not sticky). Revisit with a vendor's published alarm table when a controller that publishes one is run

reachy_mini.pending: nothing to cover: the maker's daemon defines no fault vocabulary. Its status carries one free-text `error` string (and a backend status with another), set when the daemon failed to start or a backend failed, and no code; the driver reads both, says there is a fault with a fault word of 1 and no meaning beyond it, and puts the daemon's own words in the refusal at open. What that does is held by `drivers/reachy_mini/selftest.py` (an error the daemon holds is refused at open, is FAULT and DEGRADED while it is held, refuses a command, is not cleared by a release, and is not sticky once the daemon says it is gone) against a daemon written here. The maker's own daemon was seen in that state once, by the status route and not through the driver: its first run in simulation reported `state: error` and a mesh it could not read (Git LFS pointer files in the image, found by the first run of `sim/run-sim.sh`), so the driver was not run against a maker's daemon holding an error. Revisit with a motor-level fault table if a Wireless robot's firmware publishes one

fourier.pending: nothing to cover: established 2026-10-05 (fifty-fourth session) by reading the maker's own client, `fftai/rocs_client_py` at `4730003` (v1.3.11, the commit the wire cross-check imports), whole, and the maker's published docs site, `FFTAI/fftai.github.io`. Every one of the 22 `/robot/*` HTTP endpoints the client speaks (the limit list, pvc, joint limit, joint states, stand, walk, head, waist, upper body, the sdk_ctrl calls, the state-listen calls, the hand and end-effector calls and the rest) answers `{code, msg, data}` with `code` 0 or -1 and a free-text `msg`: a per-call transport status, not a vocabulary, and the driver already refuses a call whose `code` is not 0 (`bridge.py` demands HTTP 200 AND code 0, where the maker's own client ignores `code` on most calls). The two `/control/*` camera paths are a stream URL and a boolean. `pvc` carries position, velocity and current and no error field; `joint_states` carries mode strings (`StartComplete`, `Swing`) with example values only and no enumeration; the pushed debug state carries the locomotion FSM (`Unknown`, `Start`, `Zero`, `Stand`, `Walk`, `Stop`) with no fault member; the websocket `on_error` is a connection callback and `check_motor_for_flag` sets a PD-mode flag. Fourier does publish an actuator fault vocabulary — `FSAErrorCode`, 21 bits from `ERROR_ADC_CAL_FAULT` to `ERROR_HARDWARE_TYPE_NULL`, read by the FSA SDK's `get_error_code` from the actuator's own address — but the RoCS client neither imports nor surfaces it, the GR-1's actuators sit behind the onboard RoCS server, and no documented RoCS surface carries any of its bits, so this driver has nothing to translate. The fault word stays 0. Revisit if a RoCS endpoint publishes an error field or the maker documents one

The estop flag is the driver's own latch and nothing the robot reports. Whether `lost` is a counter since boot (so DEGRADED never clears) or a window is not in anything this tree holds, and Booster publishes no table of codes the driver reads, so a table has nothing of the maker's to be generated from. gripper_fault.channel: gFLT, the low nibble of byte 2 (FAULT STATUS) of the status block, read in every exchange (function 0x17) at the exchange rate
gripper_fault.source: Robotiq's own C++ SDK, `sdk_cpp/include/Robotiq/gripper/fault_status.hpp` at 49f56f14a91327c45e10e000687ba030b595ac39 (the commit `sim/Dockerfile` pins): the enumeration, each code's own comment and the `severity()` the maker gives it, generated from the header and not retyped. The maker's four severities are the classes here: none is `ok`, a warning and a minor fault are `degraded` (the maker says they clear on their own), and a major one is `fault` (it "needs a reset (rACT rising edge) to clear"). The maker's own rule for a code it does not name is Major, and it is the table's `unmapped`. Measured against the maker's own fake gripper: that a state staged in its register model is read and acted on in all four classes (drivers/robotiq/live.py); the codes' meanings are read, not measured, because the fake raises no fault of its own.
gripper_fault.why: a gripper holds a fault in four tiers. A warning (action delayed, activation required) says the last action could not be taken yet and clears when the cause does; a minor fault (over-temperature, no communication for a second) degrades operation and clears by itself; a major one latches until rACT falls and rises again, which is a calibration sweep through the fingers' full range and so a person's decision (the `recover` motion, never the driver's own). The first two are DEGRADED and commands are accepted; a major fault is FAULT with DEGRADED, and a command the gripper is not taking is refused, because answering it OK would be success the driver did not have.

5.name: ActionDelayed: Action delayed, the activation (re-activation) must be completed prior to performing the action.

7.name: ActivationRequired: The activation bit must be set prior to performing the action.

8.name: OverTemperature: Maximum operating temperature exceeded (≥ 85 °C internally), let cool down (below 80 °C).

9.name: NoCommunication: No communication during at least 1 second.

13.name: ActivationFault: Activation fault, verify that no interference or other error occurred.

gripper_fault.unmapped_because: the maker's own rule: `severity()` returns Major for a code it does not name, "so an unknown fault is never mistaken for harmless"

controller_fault.channel: kFLT, the high nibble of byte 2 (FAULT STATUS) of the status block: the optional Robotiq controller's fault, which exists only on a gripper fitted with that controller
controller_fault.source: Robotiq's own C++ SDK, `sdk_cpp/include/Robotiq/gripper/fault_status.hpp` at 49f56f14a91327c45e10e000687ba030b595ac39 (the commit `sim/Dockerfile` pins): the enumeration, each code's own comment and the `severity()` the maker gives it, generated from the header and not retyped. The maker's four severities are the classes here: none is `ok`, a warning and a minor fault are `degraded` (the maker says they clear on their own), and a major one is `fault` (it "needs a reset (rACT rising edge) to clear"). The maker's own rule for a code it does not name is Major, and it is the table's `unmapped`. Measured against the maker's own fake gripper: that a state staged in its register model is read and acted on in all four classes (drivers/robotiq/live.py); the codes' meanings are read, not measured, because the fake raises no fault of its own.
controller_fault.why: the optional controller's faults come in the same tiers as the gripper's own, with one that is a stop: its emergency stop input (0x0C, `EmergencyStop`, "Major Fault (red LED blinking) - Reset is required - Emergency stop triggered"), the maker's stop chain, which is ESTOP and DEGRADED and refuses commands. Its overcurrent is a fault. Two warnings (no 24 V, no device) and a minor fault (communication not ready) are DEGRADED. The fault word is the whole byte, so a controller code reads as its nibble in the high half.

4.name: Supply24VNotDetected: WARNING - 24V not detected (reconfiguration through USB is possible)

9.name: CommunicationNotReady: MINOR FAULT (red LED continuous) - Communication is not ready

12.name: EmergencyStop: Major Fault (red LED blinking) – Reset is required - Emergency stop triggered

14.name: Overcurrent: Major Fault (red LED blinking) – Reset is required - Overcurrent protection triggered (Gripper)

controller_fault.unmapped_because: the maker's own rule, as for the gripper's own codes: an unnamed code is Major

axis_error.channel: the axis error word in every heartbeat (CANSimple CMD_HEARTBEAT), bytes 0-3 little-endian, read every cycle
axis_error.source: ODrive Robotics' own CAN database, `tools/odrive-cansimple.dbc` VAL_ 1 Axis_Error at 3a2e4dd1 (2026-01-20, the pin `drivers/odrive/layout_check.py` holds): 13 entries, generated from the DBC and not retyped, with `tools/odrive/enums.py` AXIS_ERROR_* imported unmodified as the second opinion on every value. Read, not measured: the maker's firmware raises these on events this repository cannot cause, and ODrive publishes no simulator.
axis_error.why: every nonzero word is a latched axis fault: the axis applies no setpoint until a person clears it at the drive, and this driver never sends CLEAR_ERRORS (it is board-wide in the firmware). ESTOP_REQUESTED is the same case — the stop the driver itself latches, or another master's on a shared bus — and a nonzero word of any shape faults identically, which the probes hold.
axis_error.unmapped_because: the word is a bitset the driver reads whole (`if axis.axis_error`, carried verbatim): a bit the table does not define is a fault from a firmware newer than this table, and masking it to healthy would clear a fault nobody read. The probes are single undefined bits spread across the word, the top bit included.

not_covered.what: the axis state byte: anything but closed loop
not_covered.why: the driver reads the state as armed-or-not: anything but closed loop is DEGRADED with commands refused while the driver re-asks for closed loop on every command. That pair is no class the contract names — degraded takes commands, and fault needs a FAULT bit with a nonzero word, for which no maker code exists (0 is §24's healthy). The refusal is loud, the re-arm is asked every cycle, and the state arrives on the next heartbeat, so an axis stuck out of closed loop reads degraded-with-refusals, never silent and never healthy.

not_covered.what: the motor, encoder, controller and sensorless error words, and the heartbeat's three flag bytes
not_covered.why: the driver reads the axis word and the state and never requests the subsystem words, and the firmware's own propagation makes that complete for every fault it stops for. Every encoder and sensorless error sets its axis bit at the set site (encoder.cpp set_error, sensorless_estimator.cpp); every controller error returns false out of Controller::update into ERROR_CONTROLLER_FAILED (main.cpp) or refuses closed loop (INVALID_LOAD_ENCODER, read as unarmed); every motor error goes through disarm_with_error into ERROR_MOTOR_FAILED except five that cannot fault a closed loop silently — BRAKE_RESISTOR_DISARMED and PHASE_INDUCTANCE_OUT_OF_RANGE surface as unarmed or INVALID_STATE, and UNKNOWN_TORQUE, UNKNOWN_PHASE_VEL and CURRENT_SENSE_SATURATION are latched advisories the firmware runs through (the first latches on every boot in IDLE, before its source connects). Reading the flags as faults would fault healthy hardware.
